rationale: Both call for thanksgiving to the Lord and give His enduring mercy as the reason. The psalm says He is good; Chronicles uses the wording it is good, which is preserved without making the two clauses identical.
The psalm addresses those the Lord redeemed from an enemy's hand. Zechariah's prophecy describes salvation from enemies and rescue from their hand in connection with God's remembered covenant.
Both describe God's gathering a dispersed people from named directions. East, west and north correspond directly; the psalm's sea and Isaiah's southwest retain their different wording.

The wanderers' waterless wilderness corresponds to the fearful wilderness through which the Lord led Israel, explicitly marked by thirst and absence of water. The psalm's unnamed travelers are not assigned a particular journey.

relationship: Hunger and thirst in the wilderness
rationale: The psalm's hungry and thirsty travelers correspond to the needs recalled in Nehemiah's prayer: shortage of food and thirst answered by heavenly bread and water from a rock.

The cry to the Lord in affliction and rescue from distress recur in the prison scene. This same-chapter refrain connects the wandering and imprisoned groups without identifying them as the same people.

God guides the travelers along a straight way to an inhabited city. Isaiah describes a holy road on which the scattered do not wander and the redeemed travel toward Zion; both join guided travel to arrival, while only Isaiah names Zion.

The call to acknowledge the Lord's mercies and wonders to human beings recurs after the prisoners' rescue. The identical refrain links gratitude for finding a way with gratitude for release from bonds.

relationship: Hungry people filled with good things
rationale: Mary's song repeats the combination of hungry people, filling and good things. The psalm describes satisfying an empty and hungry soul, while Mary's song also contrasts the rich sent away empty.
Both depict people in bonds and darkness. The psalm describes their condition, including death's shadow and iron; Isaiah names bringing bound people and those sitting in darkness out of prison.

The prisoners' rejection of God's oracles and counsel corresponds to Wisdom's accusation that her counsel and reproof were disregarded. Both place that rejection before distress; Proverbs' speaker is personified Wisdom.
The exhausted prisoners have no helper, matching the other psalm's plea that God remain near because affliction is near and no one helps. Both make helplessness part of an appeal for divine rescue.
The prisoners' cry and deliverance repeat in the following scene of people nearing death. The same-chapter refrain connects the distinct dangers through prayer answered by the Lord.
The Lord brings people out of darkness and breaks their bonds in the psalm; Isaiah addresses those in bonds with Come out and those in darkness with a command to be revealed.
The thanksgiving refrain following liberation from prison returns after healing. Both name the Lord's mercies and wonders to human beings, linking these separate rescue scenes.

relationship: Bronze doors and iron bars broken
rationale: The distinctive paired images of shattered bronze gates or doors and broken iron bars occur in both passages. Isaiah addresses Cyrus in context, while the psalm celebrates the Lord's liberation without naming him.
Both connect wrongdoing with being humbled and a changed way. The psalm reports help out of a lawless way, while Psalm 118's speaker says he did wrong before being humbled and then kept God's saying.

Both describe disruption of eating while death approaches. Their symptoms differ: the psalm's sufferers abhor food, whereas Elihu's described sufferer desires food but cannot receive it; that difference is not erased.
The endangered sufferers' cry to the Lord and salvation from distress recur among the storm-tossed sailors. The refrain links rescue from approaching death with rescue at sea.
The psalm says God sent His word and healed the sufferers. Wisdom identifies the Lord's word, rather than herb or poultice, as what healed, making the word's healing action the particular connection.

The centurion's request that Jesus only speak a word and his servant will be healed corresponds to the psalm's word sent to heal. The later narrative supplies a particular instance of trust in effective healing speech.
The call to acknowledge the Lord's mercies and wonders returns after the sea rescue. It connects thanksgiving by the healed sufferers with thanksgiving by the sailors.
Both explicitly name a sacrifice of praise. The psalm joins it to joyful proclamation of God's works; Hebrews describes it as the fruit of lips confessing His name through Jesus.

The psalm introduces people working aboard ships on many waters before describing the storm. Ezekiel pictures Tyre's rowers leading her into much water before a wind shatters her; the working voyage and storm setting correspond without identifying the vessels.
The psalm says the sailors saw the Lord's wonders in the deep. Jonah narrates a particular sea marvel, the cessation of its tossing, followed by the sailors' fear of the Lord, sacrifice and vows.

relationship: The Lord raises a storm at sea
rationale: Both attribute the dangerous wind and rising sea to the Lord's action. The psalm describes His speech and raised waves; Jonah reports the wind He stirred and the ship threatened with destruction.

relationship: Despair during a violent sea storm
rationale: The sailors' melting soul amid the heaving sea corresponds to the voyagers' loss of all remaining hope while the storm continued in Acts. The passages describe comparable distress without identifying their voyages or equating every wave image.

relationship: Drunkenness as an image of disorientation
rationale: The sailors are shaken like a drunken man and their wisdom fails. Isaiah describes loss of sense and a hangover without wine, followed by a spirit of stupor; both use intoxication language for impaired capacity in different settings.

relationship: An appeal in a storm answered by calm
rationale: The sailors cry to the Lord and are brought out of distress. Mark's disciples appeal to Jesus while fearing they will perish, and He answers by rebuking the wind and sea.
The psalm's command quiets the storm and silences waves. Mark narrates Jesus commanding the sea to be silent and still, followed by the wind's cessation and a great calm.

The psalm's sailors are guided to their desired harbor after danger. After Jesus reassures the frightened disciples, John's boat is at the land toward which they were going; the correspondence is safe arrival at the intended destination, not a claim that John narrates the same calming command.

The psalm calls for acknowledgment to the Lord of His mercies and His wonders to human beings. Psalm 104 joins thanksgiving with announcing God's works among nations and recounting His wonders. The shared connection is thanksgiving and wonders; the source is not rewritten as an express command to tell them.
Exalting the Lord in the people's assembly corresponds to the vow to sing hymns in the midst of the assembly. Both place the testimony of divine help in communal worship.

Both attribute the drying of rivers to the Lord. Isaiah's threat expressly turns rivers to deserts and names thirst and lack of water, corresponding to the psalm's rivers made wilderness and water outlets made thirst.

relationship: Salted land as judgment for wrongdoing
rationale: The fruitful land becomes brine because of its inhabitants' wickedness. Deuteronomy describes salt-covered land that no longer grows crops and explains its ruin by abandonment of the covenant and service to other gods.

relationship: Water supplied to a dry wilderness
rationale: Both describe divine transformation of dry land into places of water. The psalm's lakes and water outlets correspond to Isaiah's marshes and watercourses in the wilderness and thirsty land.

The newly established city of habitation recalls the earlier wanderers' unsuccessful search and guided arrival. This same-chapter repetition traces the contrast between homelessness and settled life without asserting that every scene concerns one group.

relationship: Settled people planting and enjoying produce
rationale: The psalm's fields and vineyards yield a crop after settlement. Isaiah describes people inhabiting their own houses, planting vineyards and eating their own produce; both connect restored dwelling with fruitful labor.

The psalm joins God's blessing to human multiplication and preservation of livestock. Deuteronomy similarly promises blessing and multiplication, explicitly including human offspring, cattle and sheep.

relationship: A people reduced in number through affliction
rationale: The psalm describes people becoming few and suffering harm. Leviticus' threatened affliction likewise makes the people few through destructive animals; it names a particular means that the psalm does not specify.

Job's speech pairs dishonor poured on rulers with their being led astray on an unknown road. The psalm similarly joins contempt on rulers to wandering in an impassable place, while preserving the difference between an unknown road and no road.

The psalm pictures families as sheep after help for the poor. Ezekiel uses the human-flock image explicitly for multiplication and the filling of deserted cities, supplying a particular parallel to the pastoral image without inserting the verb multiply into the source unit.

relationship: The righteous see and rejoice or laugh
rationale: The upright see and rejoice in the psalm. Eliphaz describes the righteous seeing and laughing at the overthrow of the unjust; the resemblance concerns their response, and his speech is not treated as a new divine pronouncement about Job.

Both conclude by asking who is wise enough to understand these things. The psalm directs understanding to the Lord's mercies; Hosea directs it to His straight ways and the different responses of righteous and impious people.

The doubled declaration that the heart is ready and the resolve to sing and make music recur in Psalm 56. Psalm 107 adds in my glory; the shared wording does not establish that the psalms describe the same occasion.

relationship: Repeated summons to instruments at dawn
rationale: Both summon the psaltery and lyre to awake and declare that the speaker will awake at dawn. Psalm 56 also addresses my glory; the distinctive instrumental and dawn sequence is retained in both.

relationship: Repeated praise among peoples and nations
rationale: Both promise thanksgiving to the Lord among peoples and music among nations. The paired audiences and paired acts of praise form a close literary parallel.

relationship: Mercy reaching heaven and truth the clouds
rationale: Both describe the scale of God's mercy and truth through heavens and clouds. Psalm 107 says mercy is great above the heavens, while Psalm 56 says it was magnified to the heavens.
Both ask that God be exalted above the heavens and His glory extend over or above all the earth. This repeats Psalm 56's closing refrain in Psalm 107's praise sequence.
The appeal for the beloved to be rescued, salvation by God's right hand and an answer recurs together in Psalm 59. The shared sequence is more specific than a general request for help.

relationship: Dividing Shechem and measuring the valley
rationale: Both introduce God's speech in His holy place and name dividing Shechem and measuring the Valley of Tents. The opening I will be exalted and I will exult retain their respective wording.

Both declare Gilead and Manasseh Mine, describe Ephraim in relation to the head, and name Judah My king. The shared sequence supports the parallel without replacing king with another traditional rendering.
Both call Moab a vessel of hope, extend a sandal over Idumea, and say foreign peoples were subjected. Cauldron and basin remain distinct source wordings within the close parallel.

relationship: Repeated questions about the enclosed city
rationale: Both ask who will lead the speaker into an enclosed city and guide him as far as Idumea. Neither passage names the city, so the correspondence does not supply a geographical identification.

relationship: Repeated rejection and absence from the forces
rationale: Both question whether God who rejected the people is their guide, then state that He will not go out with their forces. The negative statement is preserved in both.
Both ask God for help from affliction because human salvation is futile or vain. The request and its stated reason recur together.
Both conclude that through or in God the people will act mightily and He will reduce their opponents to nothing. Enemies and afflicters retain their respective wording.
Both directly ask God not to remain silent. Psalm 108's appeal concerns the speaker's praise amid deceitful opposition, while Psalm 82's following context concerns God's enemies.

The deceitful mouths speaking against the psalmist correspond to unjust witnesses rising against the other speaker. Both combine personal opposition with falsehood, without changing Psalm 26's wording that injustice lied to itself.

John's cited statement that they hated Jesus without cause corresponds to the psalm's hatred and fighting without cause. The shared wording is clear, but this link does not claim Psalm 108 is the citation's exclusive source.

relationship: Prayer amid hostility, with differing responses
rationale: The psalmist responds to slander by praying, while Luke commands prayer for mistreaters and blessing for those who curse. The shared recourse to prayer amid hostility does not erase Psalm 108's following imprecations or assert that it prays for the opponents' benefit.
Both speakers complain that good deeds receive evil in return. Psalm 108 adds hatred in exchange for love, while Psalm 34 adds the distinct phrase childlessness to my soul.

relationship: A slanderer at the right hand
rationale: The requested slanderer standing at the accused person's right hand corresponds to Zechariah's slanderer standing at Joshua's right hand to oppose him. The positional and adversarial imagery is shared without identifying the accused people.
Peter expressly cites the book of Psalms and the demand that another take the office of oversight. In Acts this supports the replacement of Judas, as the surrounding speech states.

The requested fate of a wife becoming a widow and sons becoming orphans repeats the consequences threatened against those who mistreat widows and orphans in Exodus. The psalm is an imprecation; Exodus is a legal warning.

relationship: Contrasting pictures of descendants in need
rationale: The curse asks that the offender's sons wander and beg. Psalm 36's speaker says he has not seen a righteous person's offspring seeking loaves; the contrast concerns the described descendants and does not label every hungry child guilty.

The request that strangers plunder the offender's toils corresponds to Deuteronomy's warning that an unknown nation will consume the land's yield and all the people's labors. The psalm's lender is an additional feature, not supplied by the target.

Read with Psalm 108:16, the request for absence of compassion follows the man's refusal to show mercy. James explicitly connects judgment without mercy to failure to show mercy; the psalm's extension to his orphans is not attributed to James.
The requested destruction of the offender's children corresponds to the destruction of the ungodly person's offspring in Psalm 36. The additional erasure of his name belongs to Psalm 108's wording.

The imprecation asks that parental sins remain before the Lord. Exodus describes the fathers' sins repaid upon later generations of those who hate God; both expressly connect wrongdoing across generations, with different forms and conditions.
Both speak of the destruction of evildoers' remembrance from the earth. Psalm 108 requests it as part of the imprecation; Psalm 33 describes the Lord's opposition to those doing evil.

relationship: Violence against the poor and needy
rationale: The merciless offender pursues a poor and needy person to kill him. Psalm 36 describes sinners arming themselves to cast down the poor and needy and slaughter the upright, a particular parallel of predatory violence.

The offender's loved curse comes to him and blessing remains distant. Later the speaker contrasts enemies' cursing with God's blessing; the repeated curse/blessing opposition distinguishes the two positions within this psalm.

The offender clothes himself in a curse, while Psalm 72's arrogant people wrap themselves in injustice and ungodliness. Both make a harmful moral condition into clothing, while the conditions themselves differ.

The curse is to become a continually fastened belt. Isaiah describes the ruler's loins and sides bound with righteousness and truth; the shared clothing image carries sharply contrasting moral contents.
Both petitions appeal to God's name as the ground of help or rescue. Psalm 108 requests mercy for His name's sake, while Psalm 78 links rescue and propitiation of sins to the glory of that name.

relationship: The poor and needy speaker seeks God's aid
rationale: Both speakers expressly identify themselves as poor and needy and seek God's rescue or care. Psalm 108 adds the troubled heart; Psalm 39 names God as helper and defender.

relationship: A declining shadow as an image of frailty
rationale: The speaker taken away like a declining shadow corresponds to days bent like a shadow in Psalm 101. The locust image remains particular to Psalm 108, and is not supplied by the target.

The psalm reports knees weakened by fasting, while Hebrews urges the straightening of weakened knees. The particular bodily image corresponds; the psalm's separate phrase about flesh altered because of oil is not rewritten or explained by this link.
The speaker becomes a reproach as observers shake their heads. Matthew describes passersby reviling the crucified Jesus while shaking their heads, a clear parallel of the mocking gesture.
Both petitions explicitly ask the Lord to save on account of His mercy. Psalm 108 says according to Thy mercy, while Psalm 6 says for the sake of Thy mercy.

relationship: Recognition of the Lord's hand in an event
rationale: The psalm asks observers to recognize that the Lord's hand has acted. The foreigners' advisers propose watching the ark's route to distinguish His hand from chance. This parallels recognition of divine agency without equating the events or their means of recognition.

relationship: Human requests for curses met by blessing
rationale: The psalm contrasts enemies' curses with God's blessing. Balak complains that Balaam blessed those he summoned him to curse, and Balaam says he must speak what God gives him; this supplies a concrete curse/blessing reversal.

Both petitions ask that hostile people wear shame and humiliation. Psalm 108 extends the clothing image to a double cloak; Psalm 34 identifies the opponents as those rejoicing in the speaker's troubles.
Both speakers promise to thank and praise the Lord among a large company. Psalm 34 explicitly names the great assembly, corresponding to Psalm 108's praise among many.

relationship: Same-chapter reversal at the right hand
rationale: The psalm closes with the Lord at the poor person's right hand to save, contrasting the earlier request for a slanderer at the accused person's right hand. The repeated position now holds a rescuer instead of an adversary.

relationship: Explicit quotation in a discussion of the Christ
rationale: Jesus cites David's address about the Lord's invitation to sit at His right and the subjection of enemies beneath the feet. Matthew places the citation in the question of how David calls the Christ Lord.
Mark's Jesus attributes to David in the Holy Spirit the invitation to sit at the Lord's right until enemies are put beneath the feet. Both clauses correspond directly to this psalm's opening.
Luke expressly names David speaking in the book of Psalms and quotes both the right-hand invitation and the footstool clause. The multi-verse quotation is one target passage.
Peter quotes the right-hand invitation and enemy-footstool promise while distinguishing David from the exalted Jesus in context. The link records that stated application in Acts.

relationship: Explicit quotation contrasting the Son and angels
rationale: Hebrews cites the right-hand invitation and enemy-footstool promise while asking which angel ever received it. The shared words form the stated comparison in Hebrews, rather than a new identification supplied by this tracker.

relationship: Royal authority from Zion and a rod
rationale: Both associate appointed royal authority with Zion and a rod. Psalm 109 sends the rod of power from Zion into the midst of enemies; Psalm 2 names the king on Zion and an iron rod over the nations.

relationship: Divine begetting language in royal speech
rationale: Both royal passages contain the Lord's declaration I begot you. Psalm 109 specifies from the womb before the morning star, while Psalm 2 says today; the parallel preserves these different temporal formulations.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the Melchizedek priesthood
rationale: Hebrews quotes the declaration of priesthood according to Melchizedek's order in its explanation of Christ's appointment as high priest. Its for the age and the psalm's for ever retain their source wording.

relationship: The Melchizedek declaration applied to Jesus
rationale: Hebrews names Jesus as the forerunner who entered within the veil and became high priest according to Melchizedek's order. That named order and enduring priesthood directly recall the psalm's declaration.
Hebrews introduces as testimony the declaration that the addressed person is a priest for the age according to Melchizedek's order. It repeats the psalm's distinctive priesthood formula.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the divine oath
rationale: Hebrews quotes both the Lord's oath without change of mind and the enduring priesthood declaration. The target emphasizes the oath as the distinction from priests appointed without one.

Genesis names Melchizedek king of Salem and priest of God Most High. This supplies the explicit narrative priesthood associated with the name used in the psalm, without adding an identity claim beyond those texts.

relationship: Kings confronted by the Lord's anger
rationale: The crushing of kings on the day of anger corresponds to Psalm 2's instruction to kings to learn and serve the Lord, lest He become angry and they perish from a righteous way. The shared kings-and-divine-anger connection preserves that target wording alongside the source's explicit crushing of kings.

relationship: Judgment of nations and their dead
rationale: Both picture judgment among nations accompanied by slaughter and dead bodies. Isaiah names the Lord's wrath against the nations and their dead thrown out; the psalm speaks of a field filled with corpses and crushed heads.

Both speakers promise to thank the Lord with their whole heart. Psalm 110 places that thanksgiving among the upright and the congregation; Psalm 137 adds praise before angels, preserving the different settings.
Both explicitly proclaim the greatness of the Lord's works. Psalm 110 adds that they are searched out for His purposes, while Psalm 91 joins them to the depth of His reasonings.

The statement that righteousness remains for an age of an age recurs in Psalm 111. Psalm 110 speaks of God's righteousness, while the other psalm describes the God-fearing man's house and righteousness.
The psalm names the Lord merciful and compassionate while recalling His wonders. Exodus' proclamation of the divine name likewise expressly pairs compassion and mercy among the Lord's attributes.

The psalm joins provision of food with God's enduring remembrance of His covenant. Psalm 104 recalls bread from heaven and water, followed by remembrance of His holy word to Abraham; the pairing of provision and covenant memory is particular to both.

relationship: Divine strength and an inheritance of nations
rationale: The psalm links the strength of God's works to giving His people an inheritance of nations. Deuteronomy recalls His great strength in the exodus and His giving the land of mightier nations as an inheritance.

Both praise the reliability of God's revealed instruction. Psalm 110 calls His commandments faithful and His works truth and judgment; Psalm 18 calls His testimony trustworthy, His ordinances upright and His judgments true.

relationship: Instruction established for ever in truth
rationale: The established commandments made in truth correspond to Psalm 118's declaration that all God's commandments are truth and His testimonies were established for ever.
The psalm places redemption sent to the people beside God's lasting covenant. Zechariah's prophecy likewise joins redemption accomplished for His people to mercy and remembrance of His holy covenant.

relationship: Fear of the Lord as wisdom's beginning
rationale: Both explicitly state that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and both continue with understanding. The psalm relates understanding to practice, while Proverbs names the counsel of holy ones.

relationship: The blessed person delights in God's instruction
rationale: Both open with the blessed man and associate his life with willing devotion to the Lord's instruction. Psalm 111 names delight in His commandments; Psalm 1 names the will set on His law and continual meditation.
The blessed generation of the upright corresponds to the proverb that one living blamelessly in righteousness leaves blessed children. Both explicitly extend the described blessing to descendants.

The statement that his righteousness remains for an age of an age appears with household glory and riches, then recurs with giving to the poor. The repeated formula connects resources and generosity in the same portrait without making a claim that all wealth proves righteousness.

The psalm's light for the upright is accompanied by mercy, compassion and righteousness. Isaiah promises light rising in darkness when a person feeds the hungry and satisfies a humbled life, connecting the same light image with compassionate conduct.

Both describe the good or righteous person's compassion and lending together. Psalm 111's further statement about managing words with judgment is preserved rather than rewritten as a statement about managing money.

The righteous person's everlasting memorial corresponds to the proverb that the memory of the righteous is accompanied by praises. Both contrast the lasting standing of the righteous with the fate of the impious in their respective contexts.

relationship: Confidence in the Lord amid threatening news
rationale: The established hope in the Lord prevents fear of an evil report. Proverbs likewise promises freedom from fear of an approaching fright or ungodly assault because the Lord supports the person's way.

Both describe a heart that will not fear in the presence of enemies. Psalm 26 supplies the concrete setting of an approaching army and war, while Psalm 111 speaks of the established heart looking upon enemies.
Paul introduces as written the scattering of gifts to the poor and the permanence of righteousness. The citation supplies Scripture within his discussion of generous giving.

relationship: A sinner gnashes teeth at the righteous
rationale: Both depict a sinner looking at the righteous person and gnashing his teeth. Psalm 111 adds anger and wasting away, while Psalm 36 names hostile watchfulness.

relationship: Servants summoned to praise the Lord's name
rationale: Both summon the Lord's servants or slaves to praise Him and His name. The paired address and object of praise recur as the opening of Psalm 134.

relationship: The divine name blessed for ever
rationale: Both explicitly bless the Lord's name for ever. Daniel's declaration occurs as thanksgiving for the revealed mystery, while the psalm issues the blessing as a worship formula.

relationship: The Lord's name from sunrise to sunset
rationale: Both place the Lord's praised or glorified name across the sun's rising and setting. Malachi adds worship among the nations, while the psalm's geographical sweep is stated through the sun's course.

relationship: Divine exaltation over nations and gods
rationale: Psalm 112 declares the Lord high above all nations and His glory above the heavens. Psalm 96 calls Him Most High over all the earth and exalted above all gods; the shared exaltation is clear while nations, gods and heavens remain different objects of comparison.
Both praise through the question Who is like the Lord. Exodus places the comparison among gods and adds holiness and wonders; the psalm adds His dwelling in high places.

relationship: The high-dwelling Lord attends to the lowly
rationale: Read with Psalm 112:5, the Lord dwelling high nevertheless looks upon lowly things. Isaiah likewise describes the Most High dwelling in the heights and giving patience to the fainthearted and life to the brokenhearted.

relationship: The needy raised from earth and dung heap
rationale: Hannah's song repeats the paired raising of the poor or needy from the earth and dung heap. Both depict divine reversal of extreme lowliness through the same concrete images.

relationship: The raised poor seated with rulers
rationale: The purpose of seating the lifted person with rulers repeats the next clause in Hannah's song. Samuel adds inheritance of a throne of glory, while the psalm specifies rulers of His people.

relationship: The barren woman becomes a mother
rationale: Both portray barrenness reversed into motherhood. The psalm names a rejoicing mother settled in a house, while Hannah's song says the barren woman bore seven; the different details are retained.

The psalm's opening recalls Israel leaving Egypt. Exodus narrates the Lord's host going out and the night vigil commemorating that departure; the psalm also characterizes the people from whom Israel departed as foreign-speaking.

The psalm associates Judea with God's sanctuary. Psalm 77 describes the choice of Judah and Zion and the building of the sanctuary; the link does not place that building at the same time as the departure mentioned in Psalm 113:1.

relationship: The sea withdraws at the exodus
rationale: The psalm personifies the sea as seeing and fleeing. Exodus narrates the Lord driving it back, splitting its waters and allowing Israel to cross on dry ground, supplying the narrative counterpart to that poetic image.

The psalm's Jordan turning backward corresponds to Joshua's account of the incoming waters standing and the downstream flow ceasing as Israel crosses. The poetic turning and the narrative description retain their different forms.

Both personify mountains and hills as leaping. The psalm compares them to rams and lambs, while Isaiah describes their joyful welcome; the particular landscape movement is shared without identifying the occasions.

relationship: Same-chapter question echoes the water imagery
rationale: The question to the sea and Jordan repeats the preceding statement that the sea fled and the Jordan turned backward. This same-chapter poetic echo changes the description into direct address.

relationship: Same-chapter question echoes the animal similes
rationale: The direct question to mountains and hills repeats their skipping like rams and lambs. It is a deliberate same-chapter repetition of the landscape similes in interrogative form.

relationship: Earth and mountains shake before the Lord
rationale: Deborah and Barak's song describes the earth and mountains shaking at the Lord's going forth. The psalm similarly states that the earth was shaken before the Lord, the God of Jacob.

The psalm describes the rock becoming a source of water. Exodus gives the particular narrative of the rock at Horeb producing water when Moses strikes it at God's command, without requiring the psalm to name that location.

relationship: Another narrated provision of rock water
rationale: Numbers narrates abundant water coming from the rock for the congregation and livestock. It supplies a second explicit rock-water passage corresponding to the psalm's image, without conflating it with the Horeb account.

relationship: God acts for His name rather than the people
rationale: The psalm asks that glory go to God's name, not to us. Ezekiel says God's action is not for Israel but for His holy name among the nations; the contrast between the people and the divine name is explicit in both.

relationship: The nations ask where Israel's God is
rationale: The same hostile question, Where is their God, appears in Joel's priests' plea against national reproach. Both prayers appeal to God in view of what surrounding nations might say.

relationship: God does what He wills in heaven and earth
rationale: Both declare that the Lord did everything He wished in heaven and on earth. Psalm 134 extends the list to seas and deeps, while Psalm 113 begins by affirming God's heavenly place.
Both describe the nations' idols as silver and gold and the works of human hands. The material and human workmanship recur together.

relationship: Repeated speechless mouths and sightless eyes
rationale: Both passages give idols mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see. The identical paired faculties form part of the two psalms' extended idol comparison.

relationship: Repeated deaf ears and unresponsive noses
rationale: The idols' ears that do not hear and noses that do not smell recur in Psalm 134's longer unit. Both retain the bodily faculties and their failure to function.

relationship: Repeated powerless hands, feet and throat
rationale: Psalm 134's longer unit repeats the hands that do not touch, feet that do not walk and throat that produces no sound. These bodily faculties are powerless in both idol portraits.

relationship: Repeated fate of idol makers and their trusters
rationale: Both ask that those making the idols and those trusting them become like them. The shared consequence completes the preceding description of the idols' inability to act.

relationship: The house of Israel in corresponding worship lists
rationale: Both explicitly address or describe the house of Israel in a sequence that also names Aaron's house. Psalm 113 describes its hope in the Lord, while Psalm 134 commands it to bless Him.

relationship: The house of Aaron in corresponding worship lists
rationale: Aaron's house follows Israel's house in both passages. The psalm describes its hope and the Lord's help, while Psalm 134 calls the same named house to bless the Lord.

relationship: Those fearing the Lord in corresponding worship lists
rationale: Those who fear the Lord appear after the named houses in both psalms' worship sequences. Here they hope in the Lord as helper and defender; Psalm 134 summons them to bless Him.

The houses of Israel and Aaron, previously described as hoping in the Lord, reappear together as recipients of His remembrance and blessing. This same-chapter progression connects the named groups across the two stanzas.

The people who fear the Lord, already described as hoping in Him, now receive blessing, small together with great. The repeated group links trust and blessing while adding explicit inclusion of the small and great.

The request that the Lord add to the people and their sons corresponds to Moses' wish that the Lord make the people a thousand times more numerous and bless them. Both explicitly pray for increase from God.

relationship: Blessing by the Maker of heaven and earth
rationale: The psalm identifies the blessing's giver as the Lord who made heaven and earth. Melchizedek likewise blesses Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth, coupling blessing with the same creative scope.

relationship: The earth entrusted to human beings
rationale: The earth given to human beings corresponds to God's blessing commissioning humanity to fill and subdue it and exercise rule over its creatures. Genesis describes the human commission rather than repeating the psalm's separate heaven-of-heaven clause.

relationship: The dead and those in Hades do not praise
rationale: Hezekiah's prayer expressly says those in Hades do not praise and the dead do not bless God. It corresponds to the psalm's denial of praise by the dead and those descending into Hades.
The psalm contrasts the living who bless the Lord with the preceding dead. Hezekiah's prayer makes the same contrast by saying the living will bless God, as he himself does.

Psalm 114 anticipates the Lord hearing the voice of petition. Psalm 65 reports that God heard and attended to the sound of petition and did not turn prayer away; the future expectation and reported answer remain distinct.
The report that the Lord inclined His ear corresponds to Psalm 85's request that He incline His ear and hear. Both use the same listening image in a personal appeal.

relationship: Death and Hades surround the speaker
rationale: Both describe death and Hades as surrounding dangers. Psalm 17 names birth pangs of death and Hades and traps of death, closely paralleling the psalm's pangs, dangers and affliction.

relationship: Calling to the Lord from distress
rationale: After describing death's surrounding dangers, both speakers call upon the Lord. Psalm 114 gives the request to rescue the soul, while Psalm 17 recounts the cry being heard.

The psalm calls the Lord merciful and righteous and says God shows mercy. Exodus' proclamation describes Him as compassionate and merciful, preserving righteousness and showing mercy, joining the same mercy and righteousness themes.

The Lord's guarding of little children corresponds to Jesus' warning not to despise little ones because their angels behold His Father's face. The connection concerns divine regard for the little ones, without replacing the psalm's children with another edition's wording.

The address to the soul to return to rest corresponds to Jesus' invitation to the burdened and His promise of rest for their souls. The psalm describes received benefit, while Matthew presents an invitation to learn from Jesus.

relationship: Rescue from death and feet from slipping
rationale: Both explicitly describe the soul rescued from death and feet kept from slipping. Psalm 114 adds eyes rescued from tears, retaining an additional detail not found in the target.

relationship: Being pleasing before God among the living
rationale: Both connect deliverance with being pleasing before God among the living. Psalm 114 says land of the living and Psalm 55 says light of the living; those distinct expressions are preserved.

relationship: Explicit quotation linking belief and speech
rationale: Paul introduces as written I believed, therefore I spoke and applies the sequence to his own believing and speaking. This directly cites the opening clause of the psalm's unit.

Romans repeats the statement that every human being is a liar while affirming God's truth. The psalm places it in the speaker's bewilderment; Romans' following formally introduced quotation is a separate clause about God's justification.

relationship: Returning to God what comes from Him
rationale: The psalm asks what can be repaid to the Lord for His benefits. David's thanksgiving asks how the people could offer so willingly and answers that everything is God's and their gift comes from His own; both frame human giving as a response to divine provision.

relationship: The righteous in death remain valued before God
rationale: The psalm calls the death of God's holy ones precious before Him. Wisdom contrasts the foolish view of the righteous person's departure as destruction with their peace in God's hand and hope of immortality, offering a particular divine-versus-human valuation of that death.

relationship: God's servant and the son of His maidservant
rationale: Both speakers identify themselves through service to God and their mother's status as His servant. Psalm 115 reports bonds torn apart, while Psalm 85 asks for saving might; the shared servant-and-mother formula is explicit.
The promised sacrifice of praise corresponds to Hebrews' instruction to offer God a sacrifice of praise through Jesus, described there as lips confessing His name.

relationship: Vows repaid before the worshiping people
rationale: Both speakers promise to repay vows publicly. Psalm 115 specifies all the Lord's people, while Psalm 21 places the vows before those who fear Him in a great assembly.

The location of Psalm 115's praise and vow payment is the Lord's courts in Jerusalem. Psalm 99 explicitly calls worshipers to enter His courts with hymns and thanksgiving, a corresponding setting and act of worship.

relationship: Explicit quotation inviting all nations to praise
rationale: Romans quotes the call for all Gentiles and peoples to praise the Lord in its discussion of Gentiles glorifying God for mercy. Both universal groups in the psalm's summons are retained.
Both pair the Lord's mercy with the permanence of His truth. Psalm 116 says truth remains for ever, while Psalm 99 extends it through generation after generation.
Both call for thanksgiving to the Lord and affirm His mercy for ever. The psalm's He is good and Chronicles' it is good are preserved as different wordings in the shared formula.

relationship: Israel's house in a repeated worship sequence
rationale: Israel's house begins a sequence followed by Aaron's house and those who fear the Lord in both psalms. Psalm 117 asks it to proclaim enduring mercy; Psalm 113 describes its hope in the Lord.

relationship: Aaron's house in a repeated worship sequence
rationale: Aaron's house occupies the corresponding place after Israel in both lists. Here it is summoned to affirm the Lord's enduring mercy; in Psalm 113 it hopes in Him as helper and defender.

relationship: God-fearers in a repeated worship sequence
rationale: Those fearing the Lord follow the named houses in both sequences. Psalm 117 calls them to declare His enduring mercy, and Psalm 113 describes their hope in His help.

The Lord's answer gives the afflicted speaker room to breathe. Psalm 17 likewise joins affliction to the Lord's support and being brought into a spacious place, using spatial relief to describe rescue.
Hebrews expressly quotes the Lord as helper and the refusal to fear what a human being will do. The quoted confession reproduces this verse's assurance.

The psalm joins the Lord's help with looking upon enemies. Psalm 53 similarly joins rescue from affliction with the speaker's eye having looked upon enemies; the future and reported actions remain distinct.

relationship: Trust in the Lord contrasted with trust in humans
rationale: The preference for trusting the Lord over a human corresponds to Jeremiah's contrasting curse on human-dependent hope and blessing on trust in the Lord. Both make the alternatives explicit.

relationship: Hope in God rather than rulers
rationale: Both contrast reliance on rulers with hope in God. Psalm 145 explains the rulers' lack of salvation and mortality, then calls happy the person whose helper and hope is God.

The surrounding enemies and defense in the Lord's name recur immediately with an intensified doubling of surrounded. This is a same-chapter refrain, not an identification of a particular national battle.

The speaker surrounded by attackers corresponds to Psalm 21's encirclement by a gathering of evildoers. Psalm 21 uses dog imagery, while Psalm 117:11 emphasizes warding attackers off in the Lord's name; their attackers are not identified as one group.

Both compare hostile action to bees. The psalm describes surrounding enemies warded off in the Lord's name; Deuteronomy recalls Amorites pursuing and wounding disobedient Israel, so the shared simile does not imply a shared outcome.

relationship: The Lord supports a falling person
rationale: The speaker describes being pushed over so as to fall and the Lord taking hold of him. Psalm 36 describes a fall without being dashed down because the Lord supports the person's hand. Both link falling with the Lord's supporting hold.

relationship: The Lord becomes the speaker's salvation
rationale: Both join praise of the Lord with the declaration that He became the speaker's salvation. Psalm 117 names strength and hymn; Isaiah names glory and praise, retaining the related but different descriptors.

The song at the sea says God became a helper and shelter for salvation and promises to glorify and exalt Him. This corresponds to the psalm's Lord as strength, hymn and salvation without importing a different edition's strength-and-song wording into Exodus.

relationship: The Lord's mighty right hand praised
rationale: The rejoicing tents proclaim the Lord's right hand doing a mighty work. The sea song similarly praises His right hand glorified in strength and shattering enemies.

relationship: Repeated praise of the powerful right hand
rationale: The Lord's right hand doing mighty work corresponds again to the sea song's right hand glorified in strength. The psalm also says it lifted the speaker high, a clause not supplied by Exodus.

The speaker expects to live and recount the Lord's works. Hezekiah's prayer after illness describes the living blessing God and children announcing His righteousness, joining continued life to testimony.

relationship: Disciplined but not put to death
rationale: Paul's description of being disciplined yet not put to death closely matches the psalm's discipline without being handed over to death. Both explicitly distinguish affliction from a fatal outcome.
Both call for gates to open and associate entry with righteousness. The psalm's speaker wishes to enter and thank the Lord; Isaiah invites a people keeping righteousness and truth.
The statement that the righteous will enter the Lord's gate corresponds to Isaiah's gate opened for a people keeping righteousness and truth. The shared entry qualification is explicit.
The thanks for being heard and for God becoming salvation reappears near the psalm's end. The same-chapter repetition links the entry-through-the-gates sequence with the concluding personal praise.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the rejected stone
rationale: Jesus quotes the rejected stone becoming the head of the corner after the vineyard parable. Matthew's single verse also includes the next psalm verse's declaration of the Lord's marvelous action.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the rejected stone
rationale: Mark's Jesus asks whether His hearers have read this Scripture and quotes the builders' rejected stone becoming the head of the corner. The citation follows the rejected-son vineyard parable.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the rejected stone
rationale: Luke introduces the statement as written and quotes the stone the builders rejected becoming the head of the corner. Its place after the vineyard parable is supplied by the target's context.

relationship: The stone saying applied to Jesus
rationale: Peter explicitly identifies Jesus as the stone despised by the builders that became the cornerstone. The target makes the application itself, rather than leaving the tracker to infer a new identity.

relationship: Explicit citation of the rejected stone
rationale: The letter repeats the stone rejected by builders becoming the head of the corner within its account of Christ as a living stone. The quotation supplies a direct literary connection.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the Lord's marvelous action
rationale: Matthew's quotation includes the statement that this came from the Lord and is marvelous in our eyes, directly corresponding to this source unit after the rejected-stone saying.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the Lord's marvelous action
rationale: Mark completes the stone quotation with this came from the Lord and is marvelous in our eyes. Both attribute the astonishing outcome to the Lord.

relationship: A day of joy in divine salvation
rationale: The psalm invites rejoicing in the day the Lord made. Isaiah describes what will be said on that day and rejoicing in salvation from the God in whom the people hoped; the relation is celebratory salvation language, not an identification of a date.
The crowds acclaim Jesus with the blessing on the one coming in the Lord's name. This directly reproduces the psalm's first clause in Matthew's Jerusalem-entry narrative.
Mark's crowds before and behind Jesus repeat Blessed is the One who comes in the name of the Lord. The shared blessing is explicit, while the surrounding Hosanna wording remains as given.

relationship: Royal entry acclamation using the blessing
rationale: Luke's disciples bless the King who comes in the Lord's name. The psalm's blessing formula is retained with the target's explicit royal title, which is not inserted into the source text.
John's palm-bearing crowd blesses the one coming in the Lord's name and calls Him King of Israel. The first blessing clause corresponds directly to the psalm.

relationship: Jesus cites the blessing concerning future recognition
rationale: Jesus tells Jerusalem it will not see Him until it speaks the blessing on the one coming in the Lord's name. The target itself places the psalm's formula within that declaration.

relationship: Jesus cites the blessing concerning future recognition
rationale: Luke likewise records Jesus telling Jerusalem it will not see Him until the time when it says Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord. The correspondence is the explicit cited blessing.

The psalm's festival among thickly covering boughs corresponds to Leviticus' festival using palm fronds and dense tree branches in rejoicing before the Lord. This is a limited ritual-image parallel; it does not identify the psalm's festival or explain its altar-horn detail.

relationship: My God addressed in promised exaltation
rationale: Both address the Lord as my God and promise glorification or exaltation and praise. Isaiah links that response to wondrous works, while the psalm links it to being heard and receiving salvation.
The final thanksgiving for the Lord's goodness and enduring mercy repeats the psalm's opening. This same-chapter framing refrain encloses the intervening account of help, praise and blessing.
